title: Starting fire from salvage: sparks, batteries and sunlight
summary: Make fire without matches from things nobody else wants: magnesium shavings off a water-heater anode rod, fine steel wool touched to a 9V battery, sunlight through a Fresnel lens or magnifier, a grill's piezo clicker, or the flint wheel of an empty lighter. Each one only gives a spark, a glow or a tiny flame, so the real work is dry tinder and a fire lay built before you strike. Burn outdoors or in a proper stove, clear the ground, and never leave a fire.

materials.item: Magnesium anode rod from a tank water heater (check it is magnesium, not aluminium or zinc)
Spark source for the magnesium: a ferrocerium rod, or the flint wheel from an empty disposable lighter
Alkaline battery: a 9V (smoke alarms, remotes) or two AA, C or D cells taped in series
Fine steel wool, grade 0000 to 0 (not stainless pads)
Lens: the Fresnel sheet from a rear-projection TV, a page magnifier, a projector lens or a magnifying glass
Piezo igniter with its lead, from a gas grill, patio heater or camp stove
Tinder: dry grass, birch bark, cattail or thistle down, dryer lint, cotton wool, curls of dry resinous wood
Petroleum jelly or alcohol hand gel, to make cotton wool burn for minutes
Cotton cloth and a small steel tin with a lid, for char cloth
Kindling (match to pencil thick) and fuel wood (thumb to wrist thick), dry enough to snap
Bucket of water, sand or loose soil to put the fire out

steps.text: Get everything ready before you make a spark: a fist-sized nest of tinder, two big handfuls of kindling from match to pencil thickness, and an armful of fuel from thumb to wrist thickness. All of it must be dry enough to snap, not bend.

Pick the spot: bare soil, sand or rock, out of the wind, with no branches overhead. Scrape a circle 3 m across clear of leaves and grass, ring the fire with stones or dig a shallow pit, and keep water or sand within reach.
steps.warn: In dry, windy weather one ember can start a wildfire that outruns you. Keep the fire small, or don't light one.

steps.text: Make the tinder fine. Rub grass or bark between your palms into a fluffy nest, shave thin curls from a dry stick, or pull cotton wool apart and work in a little petroleum jelly or hand gel. Finer catches faster; more lasts longer.

Magnesium: scrape a pile of shavings about the size of a coin from the anode rod with a knife spine or a file, onto a dry leaf or bark in the middle of the tinder. Throw ferro-rod or lighter-wheel sparks into the pile from close range.
steps.warn: Burning magnesium flares white at around 3,000 °C. Don't stare at it, and smother a magnesium fire with dry sand or soil, never water.

steps.text: Empty lighter: the flint wheel still sparks with no gas in it. Pull off the metal guard with pliers, hold the lighter just above char cloth, fluffed cotton or magnesium shavings, and spin the wheel hard with your thumb.

Battery and steel wool: fluff out a palm-sized pad of fine steel wool on top of the tinder. Touch both terminals of a 9V battery to it, or the two ends of a pair of cells to a few strands. It glows at once and the glow creeps outward; fold tinder over it and blow gently.
steps.warn: Use alkaline cells only. Never short lithium cells or packs: they can burst into flame. Carry steel wool and batteries apart, or they can set your bag alight.

steps.text: Lens: in strong sun (late morning to mid-afternoon, clear sky), hold the lens square to the sun and move it until the bright spot is as small as you can make it. Aim it at the darkest tinder you have (char cloth, rotten punky wood, tinder rubbed with charcoal) and hold still until it smokes and glows.
steps.warn: Never look at the bright spot without dark glasses. A TV-sized Fresnel sheet burns skin and starts fires in seconds: cover it whenever it isn't in use.

steps.text: Piezo igniter: fix the lead's tip 3–4 mm from bare metal that connects back to the igniter's body or second terminal, push the gap into cotton wool rubbed with petroleum jelly or hand gel, and click. Piezo sparks are weak: they light gas, alcohol and treated cotton, rarely plain grass.
steps.warn: Never click it near fuel vapour or a gas leak.

steps.text: Make char cloth for later: put squares of 100% cotton in a steel tin with a nail hole in the lid and set it in the fire. When the jet of smoke from the hole stops (5–10 minutes), pull it out and let it cool with the lid shut. Black, flexible cloth catches the smallest spark.
steps.warn: The tin is very hot: move it with pliers or a stick. Open it only when cold, or the cloth bursts into flame.

steps.text: Turn the ember into flame: fold the tinder loosely round the glow, lift it to face height and blow long, slow breaths into it until it flares. Set it in the fire site and lean the finest kindling over it straight away.
steps.warn: Hold burning tinder away from your face and hair, and drop it if it flares faster than you expect.

steps.text: Feed it in stages: lean kindling into a small teepee or stack it criss-cross, then add thicker sticks only once the thinner ones burn well. Leave gaps: a fire needs air as much as fuel.

Put it out properly: drown it with water, stir the ashes, drown it again, and feel with the back of your hand. If it's still warm, it isn't out. Without water, smother it with soil and stir until cold.
steps.warn: Never burn a fire, charcoal or a stove inside a room, tent or vehicle, or under a tarp, without a proper flue: carbon monoxide kills people in their sleep (safety_carbon_monoxide).

steps.text: Store your kit dry: tinder and char cloth in a sealed bag or jar, magnesium shavings in a closed tin, and batteries in their own bag away from the steel wool.

notes:
## Which method when

| Method | You need | Lights | Weather | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steel wool and battery | Fine steel wool, a 9V or 2–4 alkaline cells | Any dry tinder | Any; cold cells are weak | Fastest and surest. One 9V lights dozens of fires |
| Magnesium shavings | Anode rod, knife or file, ferro rod or lighter wheel | Damp tinder too | Any | Burns very hot for a few seconds. Needs a hot spark |
| Lens | Fresnel sheet, magnifier or projector lens | Dark tinder, char cloth | Strong sun only | Free for ever. Useless at night, in cloud or with low sun |
| Lighter flint wheel | An empty disposable lighter | Char cloth, fine cotton, magnesium | Any | Small sparks: needs very fine tinder |
| Piezo igniter | Clicker from a grill, heater or stove | Gas, alcohol, treated cotton | Any | Thousands of clicks, but a weak spark |

Carry two methods. Batteries go flat and the sun goes in.

## Numbers
- Steel wool: grade 0000 (finest) lights from 3V across a few strands; grade 0 needs a 9V. Coarse grades (1–4) and stainless pads hardly light at all. A fresh 9V sets a pad glowing in under a second; a flat one only warms it.
- Sunlight brings roughly 1,000W per square metre on a clear day. A 6 cm glass magnifier gathers about 3W, a page-sized Fresnel about 50W, and a rear-projection TV sheet (about 1 × 0.7 m) up to 700W: enough to melt metal at the focus.
- Small magnifiers focus 10–30 cm away; big Fresnel sheets 0.5–1.5 m away. Find the focus by moving the lens until the spot is smallest and brightest.
- Magnesium burns at around 3,000 °C. A coin-sized pile of fine shavings burns for a few seconds: long enough to light damp twigs that a match wouldn't.

## Finding the parts
- **Anode rod:** under a hex head on top of a tank water heater (teardown_water_heater). Many anodes are aluminium or zinc instead. Scrape a few shavings and hold them in a flame: magnesium flares bright white, the others don't. The rod has a steel core wire; shave the outside.
- **9V batteries:** smoke alarms, remotes, meters and toys. Many newer alarms hold a sealed 10-year lithium cell: don't use those on steel wool.
- **Fresnel lenses:** the clear ridged sheet just behind the screen of an old rear-projection TV (deep cabinet, big thin screen), overhead projectors, and page magnifiers sold with reading glasses. The sheets inside flat-panel TVs are diffusers, not lenses, and won't focus sunlight.
- **Glass lenses:** video projectors, binoculars, camera lenses and magnifying glasses.
- **Piezo igniters:** push-button clickers on gas grills, patio heaters, camp stoves and lanterns.
- **Steel wool:** cleaning shelves, hardware stores, paint and woodworking shops.

## Common mistakes
- Damp tinder and kindling. Collect from standing dead branches, not the ground, and split wet sticks to reach the dry core.
- Too little tinder, or jumping to thick wood too soon. Most failed fires starve in the first minute.
- Packing the fire tight. Leave gaps for air.
- Blowing hard. Long, gentle breaths grow an ember; sharp puffs scatter it.
- Lens: a hazy sky, a low winter sun, pale tinder, or a shaking hand.
- Cold batteries. Keep them in an inside pocket in winter.

## Variations
- **Flint and steel:** strike the back of an old file or a high-carbon blade down a sharp edge of quartz or flint to throw sparks onto char cloth. You need both hard stone and hard steel.
- **Car lighter element:** on a working 12V battery, push the cigarette lighter in, wait for it to pop, and press the glowing coil into tinder.
- **Concave mirrors:** a torch reflector, or a satellite dish lined with foil, focuses sunlight like a lens.
- Don't put a car battery and jump leads on steel wool: they arc violently and can make the battery explode.

## Keeping it safe
- Carbon monoxide comes from every fire. Fires, charcoal and stoves belong outdoors or in a stove with a flue to the outside.
- Wind carries embers tens of metres. Don't light fires near dry grass, buildings or fuel, and stay with the fire.
- Fire can creep underground through roots and peaty soil and pop up later. Drown, stir and feel before you leave.
